title: Neighbourhood Interview Project
goal: Your kid interviews someone in your community, a neighbour, a shopkeeper, the baker, the librarian, about their work and their life, then writes a short profile of them that someone else would enjoy reading. It turns a stranger down the street into a person with a story, and it's the bravest kind of writing practice: you have to go and ask first.
need: Someone willing to be interviewed: a neighbour, a shopkeeper, a coach, a family friend
A notebook, and a phone to record if the person agrees
A quiet moment and place for the interview

lesson.text: A good profile doesn't list facts about a person. It shows them: a moment, their own words, and what makes them who they are.
lesson.before: Mr. Patel owns the bakery. He makes bread. He is nice.

model.line: At 4 a.m., while the street is still dark, Mr. Patel's ovens are already hot.
'The bread doesn't wait for anybody,' he says, laughing.
He makes 200 loaves before the shop opens, and he still tastes one from every batch.
He learned from his grandmother, and he says every loaf is a little bit hers.

lesson.modelNote: Same baker, but now you'd recognise him if you walked in. When a profile sounds like a list, ask: what did they say, and what did you see?

howTo.intro: No teaching experience needed. You're the behind-the-scenes coach: you help find the person and make the first contact safe, then let your kid run the conversation.

plan.what: The reporter warm-up, then choose the person and write questions (Steps 1 and 2). About 30 minutes.
Write the profile and share it (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.q: Your kid is nervous to ask a stranger
troubleshoot.a: Start with someone you both know a little, like a neighbour or the librarian. Make the first ask together.
Ask 'Can you tell me about a time when...?' or 'What's the hardest part of your job?' Stories hide behind those.

skills.name: Open questions
skills.text: asking questions that get stories, not yes or no

skills.name: Active listening
skills.text: hearing the answer and asking the next question because of it

skills.name: Profile writing
skills.text: turning a conversation into a short, readable portrait

skills.name: Confidence
skills.text: talking to someone new in a respectful, curious way

steps.title: Be a reporter for 2 minutes
steps.why: A quick practice interview with you, then the real person to interview.
steps.kid: Your kid interviews you for 2 minutes like a TV reporter: microphone (a spoon works), serious voice, real questions about your job or your childhood. Then they make a list of 3 to 5 people in your community they're curious about, and pick one: someone whose work or life they'd genuinely like to know more about.
steps.you: Answer the practice interview for real, with a story or two. Then help brainstorm people and let your kid choose. A grandparent is a safe start, but encourage someone outside the family if they're ready: the baker, a neighbour with an interesting job, a coach.
starters: A family friend with a cool job
ask: What did you find out about me that surprised you?
Who do you walk past all the time but know nothing about?
steps.tip: Pick someone your kid is curious about, not just the easiest option. Curiosity is what makes the follow-up questions come.

levels.explore: Interview a parent for 2 minutes, then choose a family member to interview.
levels.develop: Choose someone you know but haven't talked to much, and write what you want to find out.
levels.extend: Choose someone in your community you don't know well, and write a short paragraph on why.

steps.title: Write the questions and ask
steps.why: Your kid prepares open questions, then makes the request.
steps.kid: Your kid writes at least 5 open questions, the kind that start with what, how, why or 'tell me about'. They order them from easy warm-ups to deeper ones, and add 1 or 2 follow-ups. Then, with you, they ask the person if they'd do a short interview, explaining the project in a sentence.
steps.you: Help turn closed questions into open ones: 'Do you like your job?' becomes 'What's your favourite part of your job, and why?' Don't rewrite them, guide. Then go with your kid to make the ask, and set a time and place you're comfortable with.
ask: Which question do you think will get the longest answer?
What will you say when you ask them?
steps.tip: Most people are flattered to be asked. Kids are often amazed by how quickly a busy adult says yes.

levels.explore: Write 5 open questions that start with what, how or why.
levels.develop: Write 7 to 10 questions from warm-up to deeper, with 2 follow-ups.
levels.extend: Group 10 or more questions by theme (their work, their past, their opinions) with follow-ups for each.

steps.title: Do the interview
steps.why: The real conversation: ask, listen, follow the good bits.
steps.kid: Your kid greets the person, explains the project briefly, and asks their questions one at a time, listening to each answer fully before moving on. They take notes on key points (not everything), ask at least one follow-up based on something the person said, write down any great exact words, and thank them at the end.
steps.you: Stay nearby but in the background. Don't jump in unless your kid asks. Let pauses happen: the best answers often come right after a silence. Afterward, ask how it felt and what surprised them.
ask: They just said something interesting. What could you ask next?
What was the most surprising thing they told you?
steps.tip: If the person agrees, record it. Then your kid can listen to the answers instead of writing the whole time.

levels.explore: Ask your questions, listen, and write down one thing from each answer.
levels.develop: Ask all your questions, take notes, and ask 2 follow-ups that weren't on your list.
levels.extend: Let the conversation flow, ask follow-ups naturally, and note their exact words when they say something memorable.

steps.title: Write the profile
steps.why: Your kid turns the notes into a short portrait of the person.
steps.kid: While it's fresh, your kid rereads their notes and stars the most interesting parts. Then they write the profile like the bakery example: open with a scene or a moment, use at least one real quote, add details that show who the person is, and end with what stayed with them.
steps.you: Read the draft and give feedback on clarity, not grammar: would someone who wasn't there understand this person? Is there a part that needs more? Point at the example if they've written a list of facts.
ask: How would you describe this person to someone who's never met them?
Which quote best captures who they are?
steps.tip: The best profiles start in the middle of something: the ovens at 4 a.m., the first customer of the day. Help them find that moment in their notes.

levels.explore: Write 5 to 10 sentences about who they are and what you learned.
levels.develop: Write a half-page profile with a scene, a quote and a short reflection.
levels.extend: Write a full profile that reads like a mini magazine article, with an engaging opening, quotes and a strong ending.

steps.title: Share it and look back
steps.why: The profile goes back to the person, and your kid thinks about what they learned.
steps.kid: Your kid shares the profile: reads it to the family, and gives a copy to the person they interviewed. They ask whether they captured them right. Then they think about the whole project: what was hard, what surprised them, and who they'd interview next.
steps.you: Be an attentive audience and give specific praise: 'I loved how you started with the ovens.' Celebrate the courage it took to ask a stranger, not just the writing.
ask: If you gave this to the person, what do you think they'd say?
What's easier now than before the interview?
steps.tip: Delivering the finished profile in person is the best part. Watch the person's face when they read about themselves.

levels.explore: Read your profile to someone and tell them your favourite part.
levels.develop: Present it to the family, give a copy to the person, and write what you'd do differently next time.
levels.extend: Ask the person if you captured them accurately, and reflect on how you've grown as an interviewer.

conclusion.headline: Your kid just planned, conducted and published a real interview.
conclusion.text: They chose someone interesting, asked good questions, listened carefully and turned it into a profile someone else would enjoy. Speaking, listening and writing, with a real person on the other side of the table.
conclusion.celebrate: Point out what they did: they walked up to someone, asked for their time, and made them feel heard. That's a skill plenty of adults still find hard.
extensions: Interview someone from a different background or generation
Record the interview and turn it into a mini podcast
Start a 'People of our neighbourhood' collection
Interview someone in another language, with a parent's help

signs: They ask follow-up questions in everyday conversations
They're more comfortable talking to adults they don't know
They notice the people behind everyday jobs around them
makeItReal: Ask the person if their profile can go somewhere public: a print-out in their shop window, the community board, or the local newsletter. Seeing their words on display makes both of them proud.
cta: Want the next one? This guide is one of 120+ in the Anywhere Learning library, each with your job and your kid's job at every step.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

photo.caption: At the town bakery: questions for the baker, then sourdough.

fromHome.text: My son and I went to a bakery in our town to learn about baking and about the baker. He asked his questions, then we learned to make sourdough bread, fougasse and cookies.
